idiom_name: RequestHandler / ErrorRequestHandler factories over the next continuation
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not a chain: middleware is typed as RequestHandler (or ErrorRequestHandler) from @types/express, filters are wrapped in factories returning RequestHandler, and the runtime behaviour is Express' registration-ordered continuation. Declaration merging on the Request interface is how typed per-request data travels down the chain. This is the default realization for TypeScript services that are not built on a decorator-based framework.
pitfalls: The types do not enforce delegation: a middleware that neither responds nor calls next(err) hangs the request, and Express 4 will not catch a rejected promise for you.
A typed req.user exists only in the type system; the filter that populates it must run before every consumer, and TypeScript cannot verify the registration order.
Error middleware must have exactly four parameters and be registered last - a three-parameter handler is treated as ordinary middleware and error propagation stops there.

variants.name: NestJS interceptors
variants.implementation_notes: NestJS turns the chain into a DI-managed, decorator-scoped pipeline: an interceptor implements intercept(context, next: CallHandler) and returns next.handle().pipe(...), so pre-processing happens before handle() and post-processing is an RxJS operator on the returned Observable; @UseInterceptors binds it per controller or method, and the APP_INTERCEPTOR provider registers it globally with dependency injection intact. Guards, pipes and exception filters already cover authorization, validation and error mapping, so interceptors should be reserved for response transformation, caching, timeouts and logging.
pitfalls: Observables are cold: an interceptor that builds a pipeline without returning it, or returns next.handle() without the operator, performs no post-processing.
Interceptors registered with useGlobalInterceptors cannot inject dependencies; register through APP_INTERCEPTOR in a module instead.
Guards run before interceptors, so authorization belongs in a guard - moving it into an interceptor changes the execution order and error semantics.
